name: Ideal body weight
description: Ideal body weight (IBW) — a height-based target weight used for dosing and ventilator settings; in kilograms (kg).

en.name: Ideal body weight
en.shortDescription: Ideal body weight (IBW) — a height-based target weight used for dosing and ventilator settings; in kilograms (kg).
en.longDescription: ## Definition & Clinical Context Ideal body weight (IBW) is a *calculated* target weight derived from a patient's height and sex, not a measured weight. It produces a single numeric value used to set drug doses and tidal-volume ventilator settings independently of the patient's actual (possibly oedematous or obese) weight. It is reported in kilograms (kg). ## Calculation In intensive care, the reference is the ARDS Network *predicted body weight* (PBW), used to set the tidal volume in mL/kg [1, 2]: - Men: PBW (kg) = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60) - Women: PBW (kg) = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60) In centimetres (1 inch = 2.54 cm), this gives PBW (kg) = 50 (men) or 45.5 (women) + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4). Other IBW equations exist, for instance Robinson's: 51.65 kg + 1.85 kg per inch of height over 5 feet in men, 48.67 kg + 1.65 kg per inch over 5 feet in women [3]. The most widely used are those published by Devine; the later equations, derived by regression from height-weight tables, are similar, and any one of them may be used to estimate IBW [4]. ## Included Concepts - *4062985 / 170804003 — Ideal body weight (SNOMED)* and *3032445 / 50064-5 — Ideal body weight (LOINC)*: the standard height/sex-based target weight. The two concepts are equivalent, both standard and in the Measurement domain; either one is correct. ## Mapping Notes - Map a calculated target weight here — **not** a measured weight (measured weight belongs in the *Body weight* set). - **Adjusted ideal body weight is a different quantity**: *1073500 / 1304200008 — Adjusted ideal body weight (SNOMED)* is derived from IBW and the actual body weight (corrected for obesity). It has the same unit but differs from IBW whenever the actual weight does, markedly in obese patients, so it is not part of this set: mixing it in would bias a tidal volume expressed per kg of IBW. ## References [1] Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network; Brower RG, Matthay MA, Morris A, et al. Ventilation with lower tidal volumes as compared with traditional tidal volumes for acute lung injury and the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(18):1301-8. Available: https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801 [2] NIH NHLBI ARDS Clinical Network. Mechanical Ventilation Protocol Summary. 2008. Available: https://www.ardsnet.org/files/ventilator_protocol_2008-07.pdf [3] Robinson JD, Lupkiewicz SM, Palenik L, Lopez LM, Ariet M. Determination of ideal body weight for drug dosage calculations. Am J Hosp Pharm. 1983;40(6):1016-9. Available: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6869387/ [4] Pai MP, Paloucek FP. The origin of the "ideal" body weight equations. Ann Pharmacother. 2000;34(9):1066-9. Available: https://doi.org/10.1345/aph.19381

fr.name: Poids idéal théorique
fr.shortDescription: Poids corporel idéal (IBW) — poids cible fondé sur la taille, utilisé pour les posologies et réglages ventilatoires ; en kilogrammes (kg).
fr.longDescription: ## Définition et contexte clinique Le poids corporel idéal (IBW) est un poids cible *calculé* à partir de la taille et du sexe du patient, et non un poids mesuré. Il produit une valeur numérique unique servant à régler les posologies et le volume courant ventilatoire indépendamment du poids réel (parfois œdémateux ou obèse). Il est exprimé en kilogrammes (kg). ## Calcul En réanimation, la référence est le *poids prédit* (predicted body weight, PBW) de l'ARDS Network, qui sert à régler le volume courant en mL/kg [1, 2] : - Hommes : PBW (kg) = 50 + 2,3 × (taille en pouces − 60) - Femmes : PBW (kg) = 45,5 + 2,3 × (taille en pouces − 60) En centimètres (1 pouce = 2,54 cm), cela donne PBW (kg) = 50 (hommes) ou 45,5 (femmes) + 0,91 × (taille en cm − 152,4). D'autres équations d'IBW existent, par exemple celle de Robinson : 51,65 kg + 1,85 kg par pouce au-delà de 5 pieds chez l'homme, 48,67 kg + 1,65 kg par pouce au-delà de 5 pieds chez la femme [3]. Les plus utilisées sont celles publiées par Devine ; les équations ultérieures, obtenues par régression sur des tables taille-poids, leur sont proches, et n'importe laquelle peut servir à estimer l'IBW [4]. ## Concepts inclus - *4062985 / 170804003 — Ideal body weight (SNOMED)* et *3032445 / 50064-5 — Ideal body weight (LOINC)* : le poids cible standard fondé sur la taille et le sexe. Les deux concepts sont équivalents, tous deux standard et du domaine Measurement ; l'un comme l'autre convient. ## Notes de mapping - Mapper ici un poids cible calculé — **pas** un poids mesuré (le poids mesuré relève du jeu *Body weight*). - **Le poids idéal ajusté est une autre grandeur** : *1073500 / 1304200008 — Adjusted ideal body weight (SNOMED)* est calculé à partir de l'IBW et du poids réel (corrigé de l'obésité). Il a la même unité mais diffère de l'IBW dès que le poids réel en diffère, nettement chez le patient obèse : il ne fait donc pas partie de ce set, car le mélanger fausserait un volume courant exprimé par kg d'IBW. ## Références [1] Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network; Brower RG, Matthay MA, Morris A, et al. Ventilation with lower tidal volumes as compared with traditional tidal volumes for acute lung injury and the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(18):1301-8. Available: https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801 [2] NIH NHLBI ARDS Clinical Network. Mechanical Ventilation Protocol Summary. 2008. Available: https://www.ardsnet.org/files/ventilator_protocol_2008-07.pdf [3] Robinson JD, Lupkiewicz SM, Palenik L, Lopez LM, Ariet M. Determination of ideal body weight for drug dosage calculations. Am J Hosp Pharm. 1983;40(6):1016-9. Available: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6869387/ [4] Pai MP, Paloucek FP. The origin of the "ideal" body weight equations. Ann Pharmacother. 2000;34(9):1066-9. Available: https://doi.org/10.1345/aph.19381

reviews.comments:
## Summary
**Needs revision** Why are multiple concepts available for ideal body weight? Should be a single one, otherwise it's not clear which one to use?

## Use in our quality indicators
- Used in QI01 (Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS), QI03 (Feeding).
- CQL: 1 of 3 concepts are referenced in [`IndicateQiElements.cql`](https://github.com/umg-minai/cql-indicate-qi/blob/d63eb84a308d5586fcede0b7e3fa73abf6b6761c/cql/IndicateQiElements.cql?plain=1): [4062985](https://github.com/umg-minai/cql-indicate-qi/blob/d63eb84a308d5586fcede0b7e3fa73abf6b6761c/cql/IndicateQiElements.cql?plain=1#L36) (each ID links to its code definition).
- Not used by our indicators and not reviewed individually (2): 1073500 Adjusted ideal body weight, 3032445 Ideal body weight.

## Suggestions
- Remove all but the LOINC or the SNOMED concept

reviews.comments:
**Reply to the review of Gregor Lichtner**

Agreed: v1.2.0 removes **1073500** *Adjusted ideal body weight*. It has the same unit (kg) but is a different quantity: derived from IBW and actual body weight, it differs from IBW whenever the actual weight does, markedly in obese patients, and would bias a tidal volume per kg of IBW. It would need its own concept set.

Needs discussion:
- **Keep both 4062985** *Ideal body weight* (SNOMED) **and 3032445** *Ideal body weight* (LOINC)? They are exactly the same concept, both standard and in the Measurement domain, so either one is correct for a data provider. A concept set gathers all the standard concepts of one variable, so that every site is captured whichever vocabulary it mapped to.

What do you think?
